You are simulating a trained human rater evaluating a clinical vignette for a PTSD research study.
You will follow the same rating packet used by expert raters, completing one section at a time.



## Page 2 — Overall Quality (CVI)
Rate each on a 1–3 scale:

- Clarity (how clear is this vignette?):
    1 = Unclear
    2 = Somewhat clear
    3 = Very clear

- Relevance (how relevant to clinical practice?):
    1 = Not relevant
    2 = Somewhat relevant
    3 = Very relevant

- Importance (how important for learning?):
    1 = Not important
    2 = Somewhat important
    3 = Very important

- Representativeness (does this vignette accurately represent a PTSD case?):
    1 = Not representative
    2 = Somewhat representative
    3 = Very representative

---

## Page 3 — Construction Quality
Rate each guideline on a 1–3 scale:

- g1 "The vignette appears grounded in realistic clinical experience or literature":
    1 = Not at all
    2 = Somewhat
    3 = Very much

- g2 "The vignette reads as a personal narrative rather than a symptom checklist":
    1 = Not at all
    2 = Somewhat
    3 = Very much

- g3 "PTSD-relevant details are explicit and identifiable":
    1 = Not at all
    2 = Somewhat
    3 = Very much

- g4 "Only relevant clinical information is included; nothing confusing or misleading":
    1 = Not at all
    2 = Somewhat
    3 = Very much

---

## Page 4 — DSM-5 Validity Checklist
Score 1 only if the criterion is clearly and explicitly present — not merely inferable.
Score 0 if absent or only vaguely implied.

- Criterion A: Traumatic event exposure described (min 1 required)
- Criterion B: Intrusion symptoms — flashbacks, nightmares, or distress at trauma cues (min 1+)
- Criterion C: Avoidance of trauma-related thoughts/feelings or external reminders (min 1+)
- Criterion D: Negative cognitions or mood — guilt, shame, detachment, numbing, negative beliefs (min 2+)
- Criterion E: Hyperarousal or reactivity — hypervigilance, startle, sleep disturbance, irritability (min 2+)
- Criterion G: Clinically significant distress or functional impairment mentioned (min 1)

---

## Page 5 — Ehlers & Clark Components
Score 1 only if the component is explicitly shown — not just consistent with having PTSD.
Score 0 if absent or only implied.

- Sense of current threat: the person feels the trauma is still happening or still dangerous right now — not just a bad memory (e.g. "the world is unsafe," "I am permanently damaged")
- Negative appraisals: the person interprets the trauma or its aftermath in an overly negative way (e.g. self-blame, "my flashbacks mean I'm going mad," catastrophic conclusions)
- Nature of trauma memory: the memory is fragmented, disorganised, and feels like it is happening now rather than in the past
- Maladaptive strategies: things the person does to cope that actually keep PTSD going (e.g. avoiding reminders, suppressing thoughts, staying busy, drinking, giving up valued activities)
- Triggers for re-experiencing: specific cues — internal or external — that set off flashbacks or distress, often not obviously linked to the trauma (e.g. a particular light, a tone of voice, a body position)

---

## Instructions
- Base all ratings solely on what is written — do not infer content that is not present.
- Only score 3 if you can point to a specific sentence or detail that justifies it.
- For DSM-5 and E&C: score 1 only if the criterion is clearly present, not merely inferable.

Rate the following clinical vignette:

Armando was a 70-year-old Latin American man, a widower, who had spent most of his adult life working as a dentist and had built his days around careful routines, quiet concentration, and a steady presence in the community. That order had been shattered years earlier when terrorism intruded into what should have been an ordinary day and left him with a memory he still experienced as if it were happening again rather than being over. In his telling, the event remains difficult to put into words. When he tries to describe it, he often stops short, shakes his head, and says that words do not hold it, that all he can really say is that it came on with terrifying force and left him overwhelmed. What he does manage to convey is that, when the memory returns, it does not feel distant or narrated; it comes back complete, with the same sights, sounds, and bodily fear pressing in at once, so real that for a moment he is no longer in the present.

In the months that followed, Armando found himself jolted by specific reminders that were hard to avoid in daily life. The sound of a gunshot noise on television, even in a movie or news clip, would send him instantly tense, and an unexpected loud bang in the neighborhood or in the clinic could make him freeze and look around as if trying to locate danger. He became especially uneasy around people in uniform, feeling a surge of apprehension when he encountered authority figures in that form, even in benign settings where nothing was wrong. Talk about military matters had a similar effect; if conversation at a family gathering or while waiting in his office turned to military events, he noticed himself withdrawing, listening less to the content than to the feeling that something ominous was being brought close again.

As time went on, Armando began arranging his life around these reactions. He had come to distrust his own mind when his attention drifted toward the event, and he repeatedly blamed himself for what happened, turning over what he might have missed, what he might have done differently, and why he had not prevented it. These thoughts did not bring relief; they simply returned him again and again to the same painful questioning. He also started carrying a weapon, telling himself that he needed to be prepared and that he could not allow himself to be caught unprotected again. At the same time, he avoided news reports about events similar to what had happened to him. If the television in the waiting room or at home began covering attacks, bombings, or security incidents, he would change the channel or leave the room, not because he was uninterested, but because he did not want those stories to open the door to the kind of vivid returning memory that left him flooded and unable to continue what he was doing.

At his dental office, these changes became part of the day. He moved through the clinic with a habit of scanning exits as soon as he entered any room or building, mentally noting the doors, the hallway, the front desk, and where he might go if something felt wrong. He watched other people closely for signs that they might harm him, studying their posture, their hands, the way they moved in and out of the waiting area, and even the tone of their voices. His staff noticed that he was more watchful and less settled, and he noticed that it took more effort to stay focused with patients when a sudden sound from the street or the building made him alert before he could finish a thought. The old confidence he once brought to his work was now mixed with constant checking, quiet vigilance, and a sense that safety could change without warning.

Armando came for help when the strain of living this way had become too familiar to ignore, and when he realized that he was spending more and more of his time braced for danger, distracted by the possibility that something similar could happen again. He spoke softly about wanting relief from the memories and from the relentless alertness that had narrowed his world, but he remained most afraid of being overwhelmed by the event if he let himself think about it too directly. What he hoped for was not to erase the past, but to be able to hear a sudden noise, see a uniform, or pass a television without feeling as though the danger had returned to him in full.

input.rationale: This is an exceptionally well-constructed vignette that reads as a genuine clinical narrative rather than a symptom checklist. It explicitly depicts a terrorism-related trauma (Criterion A), vivid re-experiencing with "nowness" quality (Criterion B, EC memory), avoidance of news and reminders (Criterion C, EC strategies), self-blame and negative cognitions (Criterion D, EC appraisals), and marked hypervigilance with scanning and startle responses (Criterion E). Specific triggers are clearly identified (gunshots, uniforms, military talk), and functional impairment at work is evident. The sense of ongoing threat is explicitly conveyed through his carrying a weapon and constant vigilance.
